newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Beleaguered Belgian Socialists strike compromise.
newsitem.headline: Beleaguered Belgian Socialists strike compromise.

text.p: The beleagured Belgian Francophone Socialist Party threw an olive branch to its partners in the country's ruling coalition on Wednesday a day before the government faces a motion of no confidence.

Socialist Guy Spitaels, whose parliamentary immunity from prosecution was partially lifted on Tuesday allowing him to be investigated in relation to bribes alleged to have been paid to his party in the late 1980s, temporarily stepped down as president of the country's Walloon parliament.
The Walloon parliament runs the French-speaking region of federal Belgium. The Flemish region also has a parliament.

Spitaels, president of the Francophone Socialists in 1989 when French aerospace firm Dassault is alleged to have handed the party 30 million francs ($1 million) for a lucrative air force deal, had been under pressure from within the coalition.
Marc Van Peel, president of the Flemish Christian Democrats, the biggest party in the centre-left coalition, had said on Tuesday that Spitaels' remaining in office was a "problem".
The Francophone and Flemish Liberal Parties, the main opposition bloc which has tabled the motion of no confidence in the government, have offered to replace the socialists in the coalition.

But Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, desperate to take his country into the first group of European Union nations forming the single currency at the start of 1999, has rejected the offer and insisted that his government will fulfill its mandate.
The four-party coalition is expected to survive the no-confidence motion and elections are not due until 1999.

Flemish radio said on Tuesday Dehaene had threatened to resign unless the governing parties backed his stand. But his spokeswoman told Reuters this had not been the case. "To my knowledge this was never said," she said.

Spitaels, also implicated in 1994 in the affair of bribes alleged to have been paid to the Francophone and Flemish Socialist Parties by Italian helicopter firm Agusta in the late 1980s, will now be questioned on Dassault alone.

He denies all knowledge of both cases of alleged bribery, but the conditions of the time-limited partial lifting of his immunity from prosecution only allow prosecutors to discuss the Dassault case with him.
He has said that once the lifting of his immunity ends on June 30 he intends to return to his position of Walloon parliament president.

The Agusta investigations brought down NATO Secretary General and Flemish Socialist Party member Willy Claes 18 months ago. Claes, who was Economy Minister at the end of the 1980s, also maintains his innocence.
The Dassault scandal is the latest in a string of setbacks for the government and the socialists in particular.

In December, after weeks of turmoil, the government used its parliamentary muscle to throw out a string of allegations that Deputy Prime Minister and PS member Elio Di Rupo had sex with boys under the legal age of consent of 16 years. Di Rupo had denied the allegations.
